fixes.explanation: True, baker! Jesus says, “…and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.” Beam out first, then clear sight.
That one wanders off a bit, friend. Jesus doesn't mention a pen anywhere in the verse. He says they “…may trample them under their feet, and then turn and tear you to pieces.”

Father is it, baker. Jesus says, “…how much more will your Father in heaven give good things to those who ask Him!” He starts with people who are evil but still know how to give good gifts to their children. Then He asks how much more the Father in heaven will give good things to those who ask Him.
A bear is plenty scary, friend, but Jesus names a different animal. He says false prophets are inwardly “ravenous wolves.” Sheep's clothing on the outside, wolf on the inside.
Jesus says the opposite, friend. He says, “A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, and a bad tree cannot bear good fruit.” Cannot is the word, and the verse mentions no exceptions.

Yes, baker. Jesus says, “Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.” It's a heavy line, and I won't dress it up. He is serious about trees that don't bear good fruit.
Long prayers feel impressive, friend, but Jesus doesn't measure by length. He says only “…he who does the will of My Father in heaven” will enter. Doing His will is what He names.
True, baker. Jesus says, “I never knew you; depart from Me, you workers of lawlessness!” The name for them and the command to depart are both right there in verse 23.
This one is true, friend. Jesus says, “depart from Me, you workers of lawlessness!” Both the name and the command are in the verse.

Lazy is a fair guess, friend, but that's not the word Jesus uses. He says everyone who hears His words and does not act on them is like a foolish man. The wise man and the foolish man are the two pictures.

That's right, baker. Jesus says the house “…fell—and great was its collapse!” He says rain, torrents and winds beat against the wise man's house too, but its foundation was on the rock. This house was built on sand.
That would be a lucky ending, friend, but Jesus doesn't give it. He says the house “…fell—and great was its collapse!” A house that stays standing is the wise man's house, not this one.
Just a roof is far less than what Jesus describes, friend. He says the house “…fell—and great was its collapse!” The whole house goes down.
Astonished, baker! The Gospel of Matthew says the crowds “…were astonished at His teaching…” That's quite a reaction after a long sermon.
Puzzled is understandable after so much teaching, friend, but that's not the word the Gospel of Matthew uses. It says the crowds were astonished at His teaching. They were amazed by it.
Offended might fit some sermons, friend, but the Gospel of Matthew doesn't say it here. It says the crowds were astonished at His teaching. Astonished is the word.

True, baker! The Gospel of Matthew says the crowds were astonished “…because He taught as one who had authority, and not as their scribes.” That's the reason given for their astonishment. Jesus taught with authority.
This one is true, friend. The Gospel of Matthew says He taught “…as one who had authority, and not as their scribes.” That's the reason the crowds were astonished. It's right there in verse 29.
